slides.0.title: From immigrant pioneers to the national drink
slides.0.subtitle: Harriague, Vidiella and more than a century of wine law
slides.1.title: Two immigrant pioneers
slides.1.highlights.0.title: Pascual Harriague (1819–1894)
slides.1.highlights.0.content: A Basque born in Hasparren, France, he reached Montevideo in 1838, later prospered in trade in Salto in the north, and bought the La Caballada estate
slides.1.highlights.1.title: From "Lorda" to Tannat
slides.1.highlights.1.content: The official guide to Heritage Day 2024 says that after several attempts he brought in a French grape called "Lorda" from Concordia, Argentina, in 1874, and made wine from it two years later. The variety became known by his surname, "Harriague", and today as Tannat
slides.1.highlights.2.title: Francisco Vidiella (1820–1884)
slides.1.highlights.2.content: Born in Montroig, in the province of Tarragona, Spain. After touring Europe in the early 1870s he brought back cuttings for his farm at Colón, now part of Montevideo, and in 1883 at last found a variety suited to the country, called "uva Vidiella"
slides.1.content: The guide puts it simply: Harriague in the north, Vidiella in the south, and both can be seen as founders of the industry.
slides.2.title: From immigrants to the law
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Official recognition
slides.2.highlights.0.content: President Máximo Tajes gave both men a special medal for their perseverance in solving "a problem of such interest to the country"
slides.2.highlights.1.title: Law 2.856 of 1903
slides.2.highlights.1.content: INAVI calls it the "mother law" of the wine sector: it gave the state control and inspection of all wine activity in the country
slides.2.highlights.2.title: The oldest winery
slides.2.highlights.2.content: INAVI says the country's oldest winery is in Colonia. Most sources name Los Cerros de San Juan, said to have been founded by the Lahusen family in 1854 (secondary sources, not tested)
slides.2.content: Immigrants brought the vines, and the state regulated wine early.
slides.3.title: INAVI and the national drink
slides.3.highlights.0.title: INAVI, 1987
slides.3.highlights.0.content: Law 15.903, promulgated on 10 November 1987, created the National Institute of Viticulture (INAVI), with its legal seat at Las Piedras in Canelones. It began work in January 1988
slides.3.highlights.1.title: Reform in 2009
slides.3.highlights.1.content: Law 18.462 rewrote much of INAVI's statute, placing it under a board (Directorio) and adding an honorary advisory council
slides.3.highlights.2.title: National drink, 2014
slides.3.highlights.2.content: Decree 171/014 declared Uruguayan wine "in all its ranges and types" the national drink (bebida nacional). Labels of domestic wine must say so, in a form INAVI sets
slides.3.content: From the mother law of 1903 to the national drink of 2014, the state has stayed at the centre of the wine sector.
slides.4.componentProps.slide.title: 🧠 Knowledge check
Whose surname did Tannat go by in Uruguay?
INAVI's register still lists it as "Tannat (Harriague)".
Harriague was in Salto, in the north.
Promulgated on 10 November 1987; INAVI began work in January 1988.
